explanations.explanation: A wife it is. Abraham tells his chief servant to swear that he will take a wife for his son Isaac. Isaac is Abraham's son, so this oath is about his future family. I think that servant showed up expecting a normal work order, friend, and walked out with a whole matchmaking mission.

Flocks and herds sound like a solid servant job, but that's not what the oath is about. Abraham has him swear that he will take a wife for his son Isaac. This chief servant already manages all that Abraham owns, so this is a different kind of assignment. It's about who Isaac will marry, not what he owns.

explanations.answer: Teach Isaac to run the household
explanations.explanation: Teaching Isaac to run things might be a fine idea, but Abraham never asks for it here. The oath is about taking a wife for his son Isaac. Nothing in these verses mentions lessons of any kind. This servant has a long trip coming, friend, not a classroom.

Careful, friend, because it's the opposite. Abraham has the servant swear “…that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling,” (Genesis 24:3). So the Canaanites living around him are exactly where the servant is told NOT to look. One tiny word, and it flips the whole plan.

False is right. Abraham has the servant swear “…that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling,” (Genesis 24:3). Then he says where to go instead: his own country and his kindred. Read past the word "not" and you've got the whole plan backwards, friend.

Relatives is it. Abraham says the servant will go to "my country and my kindred," and kindred means family. So Isaac's wife is to come from Abraham's own people. The servant has a family search ahead of him, friend, and I hope somebody packed snacks.

Allies sounds official, like a treaty and a handshake. But Abraham says "my kindred," and that means family, not allies. The text never says anything about alliances in this oath. It's a search for a wife among Abraham's own relatives.

Neighbors are the folks who live next door, and that's exactly where Abraham says not to look. The oath rules out the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he is dwelling. Then he points the servant toward his own country and his kindred instead. Nice try, friend, but the neighbors can keep their casseroles.

explanations.answer: The land he lives in now
explanations.explanation: You got it. Abraham reminds the servant that the LORD promised him on oath to give this land to his offspring. "This land" is the one Abraham is living in right now. The same LORD who brought him out of his father's house made that promise, and Abraham leans on it as the servant heads out.

That's the land Abraham left, friend. He says the LORD brought him from his father's house and his native land. The promise points the other way: the LORD gives Abraham's offspring this land, the one he lives in now. That's also why Abraham keeps saying not to take Isaac back there.

A walled city would make a nice brochure, but the verse never says it. Abraham says the LORD promised on oath, "To your offspring I will give this land." The promise is about land, not a city with walls. Keep it simple, friend, and the verse does the work.

Yes, His angel. Abraham says the LORD, the God of heaven, "will send His angel before you." So the servant isn't heading out with just a map and a bunch of camels. Abraham says an angel goes ahead of him on this search for a wife for Isaac.

A prophet would be a fine travel buddy, but that's not what Abraham says. He says the LORD "will send His angel before you." The servant gets an angel going ahead of him, not a prophet. Listen for the exact word, friend, it matters.
No priest in this verse, friend. Abraham says the LORD, the God of heaven, "will send His angel before you." The one going ahead of the servant is an angel. That's a pretty good scout, if you ask me.

True. Abraham says, "And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine." So the servant isn't stuck if the woman says no. But one thing stays put: "Only do not take my son back there." The oath has an exit, and Isaac still doesn't go back.

The text says the opposite, friend. Abraham says, "And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine." So the servant has a way out if she says no. The one thing that doesn't change is Isaac staying put: "Only do not take my son back there."

The well, right on target. As evening approaches, the servant makes the camels kneel near the well outside the town. It's the time when the women go out to draw water. I think he picked a spot where people were sure to show up, and that's smart planning.

Gates come up in plenty of Bible stories, friend, but not in this verse. The servant has the camels kneel down near the well outside the town. That's where the women go to draw water at this time of evening. Wrong spot, but good guess.

No altar in this scene, friend. The servant stops with his camels near the well outside the town. It's evening, and that's when the women go out to draw water. This is a stop for water, and I think a pretty good one.

explanations.answer: Offer to water his camels too
explanations.explanation: Right. The servant asks the LORD that the girl who answers his request for a drink with, "Drink, and I will water your camels as well," be the one appointed for Isaac. He's asking for more than a quick sip. That sign takes real kindness and real work, friend.

explanations.answer: Ask him to wait for her father
explanations.explanation: Waiting for her father isn't the sign. The servant asks that the girl respond, "Drink, and I will water your camels as well." The sign is her offering to water his camels without being asked. Her father doesn't come into it yet.

explanations.answer: Ask him where his master lives
explanations.explanation: Good question, but that isn't the sign. The servant says the right girl will respond, "Drink, and I will water your camels as well." Where his master lives never comes up in his prayer. The sign is about her kindness to a stranger and his camels.

Not quite, friend. The servant doesn't wait around. After Rebekah fills her jar and comes up again, he runs to meet her and says, "Please let me have a little water from your jar." This man is on the move the second he sees her.

False is right. After Rebekah goes down to the spring, fills her jar and comes up again, the servant runs to meet her. Then he asks for a little water from her jar. He doesn't stand there waiting, friend, he RUNS.

True. Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw more water. She keeps going until she has drawn water for all his camels. Ten camels and one jar is a LOT of trips, friend. I get tired just watching.

She doesn't stop after one jar, friend. Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw more. She keeps at it until she has drawn water for all his camels. That's a whole lot of trips for one girl.

explanations.answer: If the LORD made his trip a success
explanations.explanation: That's it. The man watches her silently "to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success." He prayed for success at the start, so he's watching to see how the LORD answers. I think that's a quiet kind of waiting, the kind where you don't want to say a word.

explanations.answer: If she will ask him to pay her
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says that. The servant watches Rebekah silently to see whether the LORD has made his journey a success. Payment isn't on his mind in this verse. He's watching to see how his prayer is answered.

explanations.answer: If her family will come out to him
explanations.explanation: Her family hasn't even entered the scene yet. The servant is watching Rebekah silently to see whether the LORD had made his journey a success. He doesn't ask about her father's house until after the camels have finished drinking. So right now his eyes are on her and the camels, friend.

Not quite. The text says that after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring and two gold bracelets. So the gifts wait until the last camel is done. Rebekah finishes the whole job first, friend, and then the jewelry comes out.

False is right. Genesis says, "And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels." The gifts come out after the last camel is done. He watched the whole job first, and only then did the gold come out.

explanations.answer: There's a place and plenty of feed
explanations.explanation: Yes, and she adds more than he asked for. Rebekah says, "We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night." She says yes to the room, and she's thinking about the camels too. That's a generous answer, friend, and I'd say the camels were pleased.

explanations.answer: He must ask her father first
explanations.explanation: She doesn't say that. Rebekah answers, "We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night." It's a plain yes, with straw and feed thrown in. No waiting on anybody in her answer, friend.

explanations.answer: Her father's house is too full
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, friend. Rebekah tells him, "We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night." So there's room, and plenty for the camels too. A full house would have been a rough ending for a long day of travel.

explanations.answer: His kindness and faithfulness to Abraham
explanations.explanation: That's exactly it. The servant says, “…who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master.” He's thanking the LORD for how He has treated Abraham, the servant's master. Notice he puts the praise first, friend, before he says a word about himself.

explanations.answer: Sending rain for the thirsty camels
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't in his prayer, friend. The camels get their water from the well, thanks to Rebekah's hard work. The servant blesses the LORD, “…who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master.” That's what he's praising Him for.

Robbers never come up in the text. The servant blesses the LORD, “…who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master.” His praise is about the LORD's kindness and faithfulness to Abraham. That's the whole focus of his words, friend.
